mechanism: Non-host crops starve the soilborne microsclerotia and lower field inoculum over successive seasons.
Breaking the beet sequence removes the infected residue that carries the fungus between seasons.
A three-year break from chickpea allows infected stubble to decompose before the next host crop.
Rotating to a poor host reduces juvenile population density in the absence of a feeding site.
Cultivars carrying effective Yr resistance genes block or slow pustule development.
Partial resistance lengthens the latent period and reduces the number of infection cycles per season.
Resistant lines limit lesion expansion so that fungicide programmes can be shortened.
Mass trapping removes adult females before oviposition, holding infestation under the treatment threshold.
Trap catches time the spray window and mating disruption lowers successful oviposition.
Counting overwintered adults per square metre triggers treatment only above the economic threshold.
Egg and larval counts prevent calendar spraying and preserve natural enemies.
Soil temperatures above 45 C under plastic mulch kill second-stage juveniles in the upper profile.
Sustained heating inactivates microsclerotia in the tilled layer before planting.
A dense winter cover competes for light and nitrogen, suppressing wild oat establishment.
Brassica cover crops release glucosinolate breakdown products that act as a biofumigant.
